working_definition: Dm2 is a distal medullary wide-field amacrine interneuron of the adult optic lobe. Its soma lies in the cell body rind of the medulla cortex and it elaborates a small bushy arbor with mixed pre- and postsynaptic morphology spanning medulla layers M3-M6B, covering approximately 2 columns in M6 and one column in the other layers. It is cholinergic (Konstantinides et al., 2022), a secondary Notch OFF hemilineage neuron, and is named after the canonical morphological type established by Fischbach and Dittrich (1989).

best_match.fbbt_definition: Distal medullary wide-field amacrine neuron whose cell body is located in the cell body rind of the medulla. It terminates with a small bushy arbor with mixed terminal morphology in layers M3-M6B. The arbors in M6B extend into neighboring columns on the dorsal side. The small arbors cover 2 columns in M6 and one in the other layers. It is cholinergic (Konstantinides et al., 2022).

justification: The cluster label 'Dm2' denotes the canonical optic-lobe cell type that FBbt records as 'distal medullary amacrine neuron Dm2' (FBbt:00003769). Every diagnostic feature aligns: soma in the medulla cortex cell body rind, small bushy wide-field arbor with mixed morphology in layers M3-M6B, dorsal extension into neighbouring columns in M6B, small column coverage (~2 in M6, ~1 in other layers), and cholinergic neurotransmitter identity. The cluster class (N=neuron) and region (optic lobe medulla) are consistent. FBbt:00003769 is not obsolete and has no Dm2-specific subtype terms that would require further discrimination. The label match is direct and the definition correspondence is complete.

other_candidates.fbbt_definition: An amacrine neuron that is intrinsic to the medulla, whose soma is located in the cortex of the medulla and that branches and arborizes in the distal medulla. These neurons project through the distal surface of the medulla, to form wide (sometimes very wide) terminal arborizations mainly or completely restricted to a single layer of the medulla.
